# **CHAPTER 1: Introduction** {#chapter-1:-introduction}

JD Solar is a small business specializing in off-grid solar lighting products that currently relies on manual social media interactions for promotion, inquiry resolution, and after-sales customer service. To address operational delays, lack of post-purchase support, and customer difficulties in evaluating system specifications, this project introduces a web-based, rule-based, multi-criteria product matching and fault diagnostic e-commerce platform. Built with a React frontend, Tailwind CSS styling, and a Supabase backend, the platform features a button-driven survey that matches customer budget, location, and power requirements against inventory criteria, an Online-to-Offline (O2O) quote request workflow for store pickup without online payments, and a post-purchase  dashboard providing self-service fault diagnostics and automated service request escalation for complex issues. By automating routine consultations and technical support through deterministic decision trees, the system aims to enhance operational efficiency, reduce administrative workload, and deliver accessible around-the-clock guidance for solar energy customers.

## **1.1  Project Context** {#1.1-project-context}

JD Solar is a small business specializing in off-grid solar lighting products. Its current operations rely heavily on Facebook for product promotion, customer inquiries, recommendations, and after-sales support. Because the owner handles these activities manually, customers may experience delays when asking about product details, pricing, power requirements, warranty coverage, installation, and product availability, especially outside business hours. Customers unfamiliar with solar technology also struggle to compare products and determine which solution best fits their budget, usage requirements, location, and power needs. Post-purchase, there is no dedicated platform for troubleshooting solar system issues; customers must contact the owner directly, which increases the owner's workload and delays support.

To address these challenges, the proposed system is a web-based, rule-based, multi-criteria product matching and fault diagnostic e-commerce system for off-grid solar lighting. The system features a guided product-matching module that uses customer inputs, such as budget, usage type, and power requirements, to recommend suitable products from JD Solar’s ​​catalog. This also includes a rule-based inquiry feature for common questions, an Online-to-Offline request process allowing customers to submit product requests before finalizing purchases at the physical store, and a troubleshooting dashboard for existing customers. Using a secure, customer-specific link, users can view their purchased equipment, warranty information, and installation details, then select symptoms via guided options to receive information on the probable cause, severity, and recommended actions. The system also provides administrative and staff panels for managing products, orders, inquiries, and service requests. By automating routine inquiries and providing structured support for product selection and troubleshooting, the proposed system aims to improve customer service, reduce the business owner's workload, and enhance JD Solar's operational efficiency.

## **1.2 Purpose and Description** {#1.2-purpose-and-description}

The p+

roposed solution is a web-based platform built for JD Solar. It has three working parts.

The first is a **product matching module**. Customers answer a short guided survey using buttons covering their budget, usage type, and power needs. The recommendation engine runs those inputs through a set of predefined rules and returns matching products from the catalog. For other questions like pricing, warranty, or availability, the survey handles those through a rule-based approach: buttons for the most common topics, and keyword-matching for typed questions it can still recognize.

The second is an **Online-to-Offline request form**. Since the application does not process payments, customers who find a product they want can submit a request and visit the physical store to finalize the purchase.

The third is a **rule-based fault diagnostic dashboard**. After purchase the customer will first have to agree to the terms of service. And they are prompted to put their personal details and credentials, each customer receives a unique link tied to their order. Inside is a personal dashboard showing every JD Solar product they own: the panel model, battery, inverter, installation date, and warranty. If something stops working, they select their symptoms from guided options. The diagnostic module runs those symptoms through a rule-based decision tree and returns the likely cause, severity, and recommended action. The troubleshooting flow works the same way as the product survey: button-driven.

An admin and staff panel handles product listings, order records, and inquiry logs on the backend.

## **1.3 Objectives of the Study** {#1.3-objectives-of-the-study}

### **1.3.1 General Objective** {#1.3.1-general-objective}

The general objective of this study is to design and develop JD Solar, a web-based rule-based multi-criteria product matching and fault diagnostic system for a small off-grid solar lighting business, that guides customers in selecting appropriate solar package and solar parts through a rule-based survey, facilitates purchase inquiries through an Online-to-Offline request form, and provides post-purchase troubleshooting support through a rule-based fault diagnostic dashboard while giving the business owner and staff a management panel for product catalog and order monitoring.

### **1.3.2 Specific Objectives** {#1.3.2-specific-objectives}

* Develop a multi-criteria product matching module that recommends appropriate solar products based on customer requirements such as budget, location, and power needs.  
* To develop a rule-based survey that provides automated responses to frequently asked questions regarding product specifications, pricing, availability, installation, and warranty information.   
* To develop an Online-to-Offline (O2O) quote request feature that allows customers to submit inquiries and product requests before visiting the physical store for purchase completion.   
* To develop a rule-based fault diagnostic module that identifies possible causes of common solar system problems based on customer-selected symptoms.   
* To develop a customer dashboard that enables users to access product information, warranty details, purchase records, and troubleshooting services.   
* To develop an admin management panel that allows administrators to manage products, customer records, inquiries, and fault diagnostic (service request) rules.   
* To develop a staff management panel that supports order monitoring, inquiry tracking, and customer service operations.   
* To develop a centralized database that securely stores product information, customer data, order records, warranty information, and inquiry logs.   
* To develop a responsive web-based platform that can be accessed through desktop and mobile devices. 

  ## **1.4 Scope and Delimitations** {#1.4-scope-and-delimitations}

  ### **1.4.1 Scope** {#1.4.1-scope}

  A web-based platform accessible on desktop and mobile browsers.

  A product catalog displaying JD Solar's available solar lighting products with descriptions, specifications, and images.

  A multi-criteria rule-based product matching module that filters products based on customer inputs including budget, usage type, location type, and power requirements.

  A rule-based survey that handles common inquiries through guided button options.

  An Online-to-Offline request form where customers submit their selected product and are directed to visit the physical store for final purchase.

  A post-purchase customer dashboard, accessible through a unique UUID-based link, showing the customer's registered JD Solar products, specifications, warranty information, installation date, and service history.

  A rule-based fault diagnostic module inside the dashboard where customers select symptoms from guided options and receive structured outputs including possible causes, and recommended corrective actions.

  A role-based management panel for admin and staff covering product catalog management and order records.

  ### **1.4.2 Delimitation** {#1.4.2-delimitation}

* The application does not support online payment or any form of transaction processing. All purchases are completed through a walk-in visit to the physical store.  
* The product matching module operates strictly on predefined rules. It does not learn from past interactions or adjust recommendations based on usage patterns.  
* The fault diagnostic module covers only the most common issues for off-grid solar setups. It does not handle complex or uncommon failures, and its outputs are based solely on the symptoms the customer selects, not real-time sensor data or device readings.  
* The customer dashboard is tied to orders registered through the system. Products purchased before the system was deployed or through other channels will not appear.   
* Administrators can’t update product matching rules, diagnostic rules, and electricity cost from the admin panel, changing any rules requires a developer to edit the code and redeploy the website.  
* The system is built specifically for JD Solar and its product catalog. Adapting it for a different business would require significant reconfiguration of the rules, product data, and diagnostic decision trees.  
* Internet connectivity is required to access and use the system.

  ## **1.5 Significance of the Study** {#1.5-significance-of-the-study}

  **Business Owner**

  The platform replaces the current manual inquiry process with a platform that runs around the clock. Instead of answering the same questions repeatedly through Facebook, the owner has a structured channel that handles product matching and common inquiries automatically. The fault diagnostic module also reduces the volume of post-purchase calls and messages the owner has to deal with personally.

  **For Solar Customers.**

  Customers get a faster and more organized way to find the right product. Rather than browsing unstructured social media posts, they work through a guided process that matches their budget and power needs to actual products. After purchase, they have a personal dashboard where they can troubleshoot problems on their own without waiting for a response.

  **For Future Researchers.**

  This study provides a working reference for rule-based recommendation and diagnostic systems applied to a micro-enterprise context. It also documents the rule-based surveys and chatbot approach buttons as a simpler and more defensible alternative to full NLP implementations in small-scale systems.

  ## **1.6 Definition of Terms** {#1.6-definition-of-terms}

  **Off-Grid Solar System.** A solar energy setup that operates independently from the main electrical grid. It typically consists of solar panels, a battery bank, a charge controller, and an inverter. This study focuses specifically on customers who own and use off-grid solar lighting setups.  
  **Online-to-Offline (O2O).** A business model where online platforms are used to attract and engage customers who are then directed to a physical store to complete their purchase. In this study, the inquiry request form serves as the bridge between the website and the physical store in Quiapo, Manila.  
  **Quote Request.** An online feature where customers select solar equipment, enter their contact info, and reserve items before purchasing. It provides the user with a tracking reference code (Quote Ticket) and instructions to visit the physical store to finalize payment and pick up their items.  
  **Product Matching.** The process of filtering and suggesting products from a database based on a customer's stated preferences and requirements. In this study, product matching is performed by the rule-based recommendation engine using criteria such as budget, location type, and energy needs.  
  **Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).** A security approach that restricts system access based on the role of the user. In this study, the admin has full management privileges while staff members have limited access to specific modules such as service requests and inquiry logs.  
  **Rule-Based System.** A system that uses predefined logical conditions to make decisions or recommendations. In this study, the rule-based engine powers both the product recommendation module and the fault diagnostic module by applying If-Then logic to match customer inputs with appropriate outputs.  
  **Service Request.** A formal submission made by a customer when their solar issue requires technician intervention. In this study, service requests are submitted through the customer dashboard and managed by admin and staff through the management panel.  
  **Severity Level.** A classification assigned by the fault diagnostic engine to indicate the urgency of a reported issue. In this study, severity is categorized as Low, Medium, or High to help customers and staff prioritize the appropriate response.  
  **Supabase.** An open-source backend platform built on PostgreSQL that provides database management, authentication, and storage services. In this study, Supabase serves as the primary database for storing product information, customer records, and order data.  
  **Unit Testing (UT).** A software testing phase where individual source code modules, algorithms, and isolated client-side functions (such as recommendation algorithms, diagnostic logic, and input sanitizers) are evaluated independently to verify that each function operates correctly without runtime errors.   
  **Walk-in Customer.** A customer who physically visits the store without a prior appointment. The proposed system encourages this behavior by providing product information and guided recommendations online, then directing customers to the physical store for final consultation and purchase.  
  **Web-Based System.** A software application accessed through a web browser over the internet without requiring local installation. The proposed system is web-based to ensure accessibility across both desktop and mobile devices.  
  **Warranty Tracking.** A feature of the post-purchase dashboard that displays the warranty expiration date of a customer's purchased solar product. It allows customers to reference their coverage period when submitting service requests or fault reports.  
  **Decision Tree.** A model, often visual, that uses a branching, tree-like structure to illustrate a series of IF/Else decisions and their potential consequences or outcomes, forming the logic of the rule-based system.  
  **Fault Diagnostic.** The process of identifying the cause of a malfunctioning solar product by systematically analyzing observed symptoms against a set of predefined rules.  
  **Management Panel.** A secure, role-based backend interface that allows authorized personnel (Admin and Staff) to perform administrative tasks, such as managing product listings, monitoring order records, and tracking inquiry logs.  
  **Multi-Criteria.** Involves considering multiple variables or constraints (such as budget, usage type, and power needs) simultaneously to narrow down a set of options.  
  


  # **CHAPTER 2: Review of related Literature and Studies** {#chapter-2:-review-of-related-literature-and-studies}

  ## **2.1 Related Literature**    **Foreign Literatures**    **Investigating the user experience of customer service chatbot interaction: a framework for qualitative analysis of chatbot dialogues** {#2.1-related-literature-foreign-literatures-investigating-the-user-experience-of-customer-service-chatbot-interaction:-a-framework-for-qualitative-analysis-of-chatbot-dialogues}

  Designing e-commerce evaluation tools in specific technical areas means making sure the system responds the way users expect. In a study that looked at customer service conversations, Følstad and Taylor (2021) found that looking at types of user interactions helps developers make better automated responses. This makes sure the platforms work well for both users and people who know a lot. This research shows that the survey and quote system on the JD Solar Web Portal works for two reasons. Based on the user experience rules, from Følstad and Taylor (2021) the website changes how it shows information using React and Tailwind CSS. This helps people understand solar parts through simple button-based steps. This makes the system easy to use. Helps people finish their tasks no matter how much they know about the subject.

  **Technology development and commercial applications of industrial fault diagnosis system: a review**

  Standardizing fault detection procedures within equipment platforms reduces operational uncertainty and improves user confidence in complex hardware deployments. In an analysis of technology development in fault diagnosis systems, Liu, Cichon, Królczyk and colleagues (2022) established that systematic fault detection procedures reduce errors and improve overall system availability across varied operating conditions. This literature serves as a foreign reference for the maintenance framework of the JD Solar Web Portal. Grounded in the reliability guidelines emphasized by Liu et al. (2022) The proposed system provides off-grid solar users with a standardized button-driven diagnostic interface. The engine processes solar users selected fault symptoms to isolate hardware misconfigurations offering self-service corrective steps that preserve buyer trust and maintain platform reliability.


  **A multi-criteria decision making approach to the new product development process in industry**

  Improving how users make decisions on web platforms means moving away from guesswork and subjective filtering. Instead a structured approach using multi-criteria decision models works better. Research from Reports in Mechanical Engineering in 2022 showed that using Multi-Criteria Decision Making or MCDM helps reduce confusion and improves workflows when refining products in stages. This finding is a reference for how the JD Solar Web Portal makes recommendations.

  Following the process improvement model from that research the new platform replaces messaging on social media with a multi-variable button survey. Behind the scenes the client-side engine analyzes parameters, like inverter ratings, solar panel wattage and battery storage capacity. It then calculates thresholds. Gives local solar buyers automated data-driven setup matches. This helps simplify the purchase evaluation process and makes it faster and more accurate.

  **A Literature Review on Rule-Based Systems as Decision Support Systems**

  Implementing automated decision support systems in enterprise platforms helps reduce the amount of administrative work. It also makes user guidance more consistent. Research by Savvadelli, Kiouvrekis and Kokkinaki (2025) looked at rule-based decision mechanisms. Their findings showed that rule-driven interfaces can effectively handle evaluation tasks. These interfaces give expert users clear and actionable results. They do this without needing human supervision. This finding supports the recommendation and diagnostic workflows used in the JD Solar Web Portal. The portal is built on the administrative automation framework, from Savvadelli et al. (2025). It replaces manual, repetitive social media inquiries. It uses a decision-support system instead. The platform collects customer power needs at the start. After a purchase it offers automated rule-based fault diagnosis. This improves store operations. Strengthens the client’s ability to help themselves.


  


  **An Expert System for Laptop Fault Diagnostic Assistance**

  Automating hardware diagnostic workflows inside self‑service software lets people who are not tech experts find the cause of problems without needing a professional right away. In a study on automated support tools Wee Jern, Samsudin, Aswad and Khalaf (2021) created a rule‑driven expert system that checks user‑reported symptoms through questions to spot hardware faults and give easy fixes. Their results showed that automating these checks cuts problem‑solving time a lot and saves users from paying for maintenance on small issues. This study gives technical support for the post‑purchase design of the JD Solar Web Portal. Off‑grid systems have many linked parts so regular customers often think small hiccups like inverter trips or battery discharge limits are big system failures. Using the expert system model from Wee Jern et al. (2021) JD Solar adds a 24/7 rule‑based fault dashboard. The system checks answers to button‑based symptom questions that match the clues, with proven rules and gives instant, self‑service fixes and makes warranty claims faster.

  **Recommendation Systems for e-Shopping: Review of Techniques for Retail and Sustainable Marketing**

  Designing recommendation tools for commercial platforms is a balancing act between technical precision, user acceptance and operational feasibility. A study by Stalidis, Karaveli, Diamantaras and colleagues in 2023 showed that the best recommendation tools work only when they create recommendation flows that meet real user needs and keep people using the platform for a long time. That finding is a signal that the user interface design of JD Solar Web Portal is on the right track. By applying the user acceptance principles from Stalidis and team in 2023 to a solar business JD Solar swaps informal social media questions for a simple button‑driven recommendation survey. The client‑side decision engine looks at what wattage a buyer wants and how much the buyer can spend then shows pre‑approved package quotes that give users confidence before they go to a physical store.

  **Wind turbine fault diagnosis based on a mivar expert system**

  Automation of how faults in hardware can be detected in unique energy storefronts reduces the effort needed in manual chats through the use of decision rules. According to the 2025 study carried out by Dou, Gong, Shen, and Varlamov, structured rule sets assist people in understanding faults and knowing what needs to be done, providing them with easy steps for troubleshooting. This is in line with the after-sale functionality offered in the JD Solar Web Portal. Using the maintenance automation concept by Dou et al., (2025) in a small-scale solar firm, JD Solar introduces a 24/7 fault diagnostics dashboard once products have been purchased. In case customers experience any faults with their off-grid solar kits, they are assisted via the portal to identify solutions through preset rules.

  ## **2.3 Synthesis of Reviewed Literature & Studies** {#2.3-synthesis-of-reviewed-literature-&-studies}


  The reviewed foreign and local literature and studies establish that multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) frameworks (Paradowski et al., 2021; Namoco et al., 2021\) and guided, button-driven interfaces (Kleemann et al., 2025; Mariano et al., 2025\) reduce buyer confusion and prevent costly specification mismatches compared to unstructured social media browsing. Similarly, research on automated maintenance and local helpdesk workflows (Wee Jern et al., 2021; Serrano, 2023\) confirms that rule-based fault diagnostic trees and structured ticketing accelerate issue resolution while minimizing repetitive staff workload. Furthermore, local retail studies (Capitulo & Yturralde, 2025; Desepida & Corpuz, 2025\) show that pairing online convenience with physical showroom inspection (Online-to-Offline) and reliable service recovery strengthens consumer trust.   However, existing studies and commercial platforms address these functions in isolation or rely on heavy enterprise analytics (Dadiz, 2024; Qin et al., 2021\) unsuitable for small retail operations. Existing systems lack a unified, lightweight platform tailored for off-grid solar micro-enterprises that bridges pre-purchase multi-criteria product sizing and Online-to-Offline (O2O) showroom reservations with post-purchase warranty tracking and self-service fault diagnostics, which the proposed JD Solar system provides through a deterministic, client-side rule engine and cloud-backed management portal.


  

  # **CHAPTER: 3 Technical Background** {#chapter:-3-technical-background}


  ## **3.1 Overview of Current Technologies**  {#3.1-overview-of-current-technologies}


      The proposed JD Solar platform is a modern, full-stack web application developed using client-side JavaScript technologies and cloud backend services provided by Supabase  To address the operational inefficiencies of manual social media channels and eliminate the unpredictability of artificial intelligence hallucinations, the system operates under a deterministic framework utilizing fixed If-Then Rule Engines and mathematical decision algorithms . The client-side interface is developed in JavaScript (JSX) using React, bundled with Vite for optimized hot-module replacement and production builds, and styled using Tailwind CSS alongside shadcn/ui accessible component primitives . The platform executes natively within standard desktop and mobile web browsers, ensuring seamless cross-device accessibility across smartphones, tablets, and laptops without requiring client-side application installation.


  ## **3.2 Evaluation of the Existing System** {#3.2-evaluation-of-the-existing-system}

  JD Solar currently runs its customer-facing operations through Facebook. The  owner personally handles product promotion, inquiries, recommendations, and after-sales concerns through direct messaging, phone, and walk-ins. This section evaluates that baseline against three criteria: performance, accuracy, and accessibility. In terms of performance, everything goes through one person. The owner answers every message, recommends products, and handles after-sales, so replies depend on whether the owner is free. When many customers message at once, or after business hours, they have to wait. The owner also ends up answering the same questions about price, warranty, and specifications again and again.

  Accuracy is the weaker point. Recommendations are given case by case in chat with no standard criteria, so the advice can differ from one customer to the next. Orders, inquiries, and warranty details are tracked by hand, which makes records hard to find and leaves no central log of inquiries or purchases. For accessibility, customers have to browse unstructured Facebook posts and message the owner just to compare products. A customer who does not know much about solar has no guide in choosing one. There is also no online pre-order, so ordering means contacting the owner or staff directly. After a purchase, a customer with a problem has to call or message the owner. There is no troubleshooting channel, no warranty or purchase record the customer can check, and no way to track escalated cases. The current process works for a small volume of inquiries but does not scale. It depends entirely on the owner's time, gives inconsistent technical guidance, and offers customers no structured way to compare products or troubleshoot. These gaps justify the proposed system's four modules: guided product matching, a rule-based survey for common inquiries, an O2O quote request form, and a fault diagnostic dashboard.


  ## **3.3 Technical Feasibility** {#3.3-technical-feasibility}

  The technical feasibility of the proposed JD Solar system evaluates whether the required hardware, software, and network infrastructure are available and suitable for developing, deploying, and maintaining the application. The system uses web-based technologies that allow customers, administrators, and staff to access its features through desktop and mobile browsers without installing additional software.

  The proposed system is technically feasible because it utilizes accessible development tools, cloud-based database services, and commonly available computing devices. Its architecture does not require a dedicated physical server or expensive hardware, making it suitable for the operational needs of JD Solar.

  ### **3.3.1 Hardware Specs** {#3.3.1-hardware-specs}

1. Development  
   1. Minimum: Intel Core i3 or AMD Ryzen 3 (or equivalent), 8 GB RAM, 256 GB SSD, integrated graphics, Windows 10 or Ubuntu/Debian.  
   2. Recommended: Intel Core i5 or AMD Ryzen 5 (or equivalent), 16 GB DDR4 RAM, 512 GB SSD, integrated graphics (Intel UHD/Iris Xe or AMD Radeon), Windows 10/11 or Linux.  
2. Server / Hosting  
   1. Minimum: a Supabase managed cloud project on the free tier. No self-hosted server is needed.  
   2. Recommended: a Supabase paid tier, for more storage and bandwidth and no pausing of inactive projects.  
3. Admin Web Access  
   1. Minimum: a desktop or laptop with a dual-core processor and 4 GB RAM, running Windows 10, macOS Catalina 10.15, or a modern Linux distro, with a modern browser (JavaScript enabled) and a stable internet connection.  
   2. Recommended: Core i3 or Ryzen 3 or better, 8 GB RAM, the latest Chrome, Edge, Safari, or Brave, and a stable broadband connection.  
4. Mobile User Access  
   1. Minimum: a smartphone or tablet with a modern mobile browser (JavaScript enabled) and a stable Wi-Fi or mobile data connection.  
   2. Recommended: an updated Android or iOS device with a current browser and a stable connection, so product images load faster.

      ### 

      ### **3.3.2 Software Specs** {#3.3.2-software-specs}

     
1. Development Tools and Frameworks  
   1. Frontend Development  
      1. React (Vite) — A fast, component-based JavaScript UI library bundled using the Vite build tool for hot-module replacement and optimized production builds.  
      2. Tailwind CSS — A utility-first CSS framework used for styling responsive and consistent user interface layouts.  
      3. shadcn/ui — A collection of accessible, unstyled React component primitives used for buttons, dialogs, forms, and navigation elements throughout the platform.  
   2. Backend Development  
      1. Supabase Edge Functions — Serverless functions deployed on Supabase’s cloud infrastructure that handle operations and server side processing when required by the system.  
      2. Client-Side JavaScript Rule Engine — A deterministic ruled-based engine implemented in JavaScript that runs directly in the user’s browser. It handles product matching and fault diagnostic using predefined rules and decision logic without machine learning.  
      3. Vercel Serverless Functions (/api/send-confirmation-email) — A serverless Node.js microservice environment executing transactional email dispatches using Nodemailer and server-side QR generation (qrcode.js). It manages asynchronous transmission of POS digital receipts, account verification tokens, and Online-to-Offline (O2O) showroom reservation ticket passes using Google SMTP SSL with automatic fallback to Supabase Auth mailers.  
   3. Database and Storage  
      1. Supabase (PostgreSQL) — The primary relational database storing the product catalog, customer records, order history, service requests, and inquiry logs.  
      2. Supabase Storage — Cloud object storage used to host and serve product image files.  
   4. Security and Authentication  
      1. Supabase Auth — Manages role-based user authentication for admin and staff accounts using JSON Web Tokens (JWT).  
      2. Row Level Security (RLS) — PostgreSQL-level policies that enforce data access restrictions, ensuring each user role can only read or write the records they are authorized to access.  
   5. Development and Testing Utilities  
      1. ESLint — Static code analysis tool used to enforce consistent coding standards across the frontend codebase.  
      2. Python 3 — Used only as an offline scripting environment for data seeding tasks such as bulk uploading product records and images to Supabase during initial setup; not a live backend server.  
      3. Postman — API testing tool used to verify Supabase Edge Function endpoints and database REST API responses during development.  
      4. Browser DevTools — Used for inspecting component behavior, network requests, and responsive layout testing across screen sizes.

      ### **3.3.3 Network/Architecture Specs** {#3.3.3-network/architecture-specs}

   ![][image1]

   ##### **Figure 1 \- Software Architecture** {#figure-1---software-architecture}

   

   The system follows a three-tier architecture made up of a presentation layer, an application layer, and a data layer. 

   **Presentation Layer (Frontend).** Built using React (JSX) and styled with Tailwind CSS to deliver a fast, responsive user interface. It captures user responses for product matching and troubleshooting, renders product details, and displays the administrative dashboards and the product media retrieved from the database.

   **Application Layer (Business Logic).** This layer holds the application’s core rules and state management. It has an Authentication Context to maintain secure session roles and a client-side rule-based engine that parses keyword-based FAQs. It drives the Product Matching and Fault Diagnostics workflows by running user selections through deterministic logical flows.

   **Data Layer (Database).** This is the storage and security backbone of the application. A PostgreSQL database (Supabase) manages the structured records such as product details, customer profiles, logs, and orders, while a Supabase bucket hosts and serves the product images directly to the frontend.

   **Network Protocols.** All communication between the browser and Supabase goes over HTTPS, so data in transit is encrypted. The frontend exchanges data with the backend through REST API calls, using Supabase’s auto-generated REST endpoints. Admin and staff requests carry a JWT issued by Supabase Auth, and customers reach their dashboard through a unique UUID-based link.

   # **CHAPTER: 4 Methodology, Testing and Evaluation** {#chapter:-4-methodology,-testing-and-evaluation}

   ## **4.1 Software Development Life Cycle** {#4.1-software-development-life-cycle}

   **![][image2]**

   ##### **Figure 2 \- (Agile) *Software Development Life Cycle*** {#figure-2---(agile)-software-development-life-cycle}

   The Agile Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) model was selected because the project required continuous development, testing, and refinement of multiple system modules throughout the implementation process. Since the system consists of several interconnected features such as product matching, rule-based survey support, online-to-offline requests, fault diagnostics, and management panels, an iterative approach allowed the development team to develop, test, and improve each feature incrementally based on feedback and evaluation results.

   ## **4.2 Requirements Analysis** {#4.2-requirements-analysis}

   **Planning:**  
         	The project began by identifying the challenges faced by JD Solar, particularly the difficulty of managing customer inquiries, product recommendations, and after-sales support manually. The team defined the project goals, identified the target users, and created a development roadmap that divided the system into manageable iterations or sprints.

   **Requirements Analysis:**  
         	During this phase, the team gathered and analyzed the functional and non-functional requirements of the system. Key requirements included a multi-criteria product matching module, a rule-based survey for common inquiries, an Online-to-Offline request form, a fault diagnostic dashboard, and role-based management panels for administrators and staff. Requirements were continuously reviewed and refined throughout development whenever improvements were identified.

   **Sprint Planning and Design:**  
         	The system architecture, database structure, Data Flow Diagrams (DFD), Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD), System Flowcharts, and Conceptual Framework were designed before development started. The project was then divided into smaller development cycles, allowing each module to be designed, developed, and evaluated independently while maintaining integration with the overall system.

   **Development (Iterative Coding):**  
         	The team developed the system in multiple iterations using React with Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Supabase. Early sprints focused on the product catalog and multi-criteria product matching module. Subsequent sprints added the rule-based survey, Online-to-Offline request, customer dashboard, fault diagnostic module, and the admin and staff management panels. Continuous integration ensured that newly developed features worked properly with previously completed modules.

   **Testing and Review:**  
         	Testing was performed after each sprint to identify and resolve issues early in the development process. Unit Testing was conducted on individual modules such as the recommendation engine, survey rules, and diagnostic decision tree. Integration Testing ensured that all modules communicated correctly with the database and backend services. Feedback from the development team and stakeholders was used to refine features before proceeding to the next sprint. User Acceptance Testing (UAT) was also conducted to evaluate system usability, functionality, and overall effectiveness.

   **Deployment:**  
         	After completing and validating all major system modules, the application was deployed to the cloud environment and connected to the Supabase database infrastructure. The deployed system enables customers to access product recommendations, troubleshooting services, and quote through desktop and mobile web browsers at any time.

   **Maintenance and Continuous Improvement:**  
         	Agile promotes continuous enhancement even after deployment. The team monitors system performance, fixes reported issues, updates product information, improves recommendation rules, and enhances survey responses when necessary. Through the Admin and Staff Management Panels, authorized personnel can maintain the product catalog, manage customer records, monitor inquiry logs, and track service requests to ensure the system remains effective and up to date.

   ## **4.3 System Design and Modeling** {#4.3-system-design-and-modeling}

   

   **IPO (**Input \- Process \- Output**)**

   **![][image3]**

   ##### **Figure 3 \- IPO** {#figure-3---ipo}

   

   The Input-Process-Output (IPO) model was used as the conceptual framework of the study because it clearly shows how the data supplied by users is transformed by the system’s rule-based logic into useful results. Since the JD Solar system consists of several interconnected modules such as product matching, rule-based inquiry support, online-to-offline quote requests, fault diagnostics, and management panels, the IPO model made it possible to trace how each module receives its inputs, applies its processes, and produces its outputs. The inputs consist of customer survey responses (budget, usage type, location, and power requirements), frequently asked questions, product and contact details for quote requests, selected fault symptoms, and the catalog and rule updates entered by the administrator and staff. These inputs are processed through the client-side rule engine, which applies If-Then logic for product matching and inquiry handling, generates quote tickets for the online-to-offline process, evaluates symptoms through the diagnostic decision tree, and enforces role-based access in the management panel using Supabase Authentication and Row Level Security. The outputs are the matched product recommendations and automated answers, quote ticket codes with store pickup instructions, diagnostic results showing the probable cause, severity level, and recommended action (with escalation to a service request for high-severity cases), and updated product, order, and inquiry records. Finally, the feedback loop shows that staff notes, inquiry logs, and service history are reviewed by the administrator to refine the product data, matching rules, and diagnostic rules, which keeps the system accurate and up to date.

##### **Figure 5 \- Use Case Diagram** {#figure-5---use-case-diagram}

The Use Case Diagram illustrates the interactions between the users and the JD Solar Web-Based System. It identifies three main actors: Customer, Admin, and Staff, each with different responsibilities and access to the system's features.

The Customer can browse the product catalog, receive product recommendations based on their needs and budget, ask product-related inquiries, submit quoate requests, view equipment and warranty information, perform fault diagnostics, and submit service requests.

The Admin is responsible for managing products, customer records, and diagnostic rules. These functions help ensure that product information and system records remain organized and updated.

The Staff can monitor orders, track customer inquiries, and manage service requests. These functions help staff provide customer support and keep track of ongoing transactions and service-related concerns.

Overall, the Use Case Diagram provides an overview of the system's main functions and shows how each actor interacts with them. The system supports product selection, inquiry management, and troubleshooting while the final purchase and payment are handled outside the web system.

### **4.3.3 Data Flow Diagram** {#4.3.3-data-flow-diagram}

![][image5]

##### **Figure 6 \- Data Flow Diagram** {#figure-6---data-flow-diagram}

**Data Flow Diagram Level 0**

The Level 0 Data Flow Diagram illustrates how information is exchanged within the JD Solar Web-Based System. It includes three external entities: Customer, Admin, and Staff, along with four main processes and nine data stores. The diagram explains how customer inputs are processed, how records are stored, and how the system supports product recommendations, quote requests, fault diagnosis, and administrative tasks.

### 

**Processes**

**1.0 Product Matching and Rule-Based Inquiry**

This process handles the customer's product preferences and inquiries. Customers answer a guided survey about their budget, intended usage, location, and power requirements, or enter keywords related to their questions. The system checks the product catalog in D1 (Products) and applies predefined If-Then rules to identify suitable products and provide answers to common questions about pricing, warranty, availability, and installation. The survey results and recommended products are recorded in D2 (Product Matching Logs).

**2.0 Online-to-Offline Request Processing**

This process manages customer  quote  requests and product orders. Customers provide their chosen products and contact information, while the system retrieves the necessary product details from D1 (Products). Customer information is saved in D4 (Customers), and the submitted requests and order details are stored in D3 (Orders & Order Items). After submission, the customer receives a reference code and instructions for completing the purchase at the physical store. An automated transactional email dispatch process triggers, transmitting the reservation code and digital pass receipt to the customer's specified email address. Payments are not handled by the web-based system.

**3.0 Customer Dashboard and Fault Diagnostics**

This process allows customers to access their product information through a unique UUID-based dashboard link. The system checks the customer's records in D4 (Customers) and retrieves information about their registered products, installation dates, and warranty coverage from D5 (Customer Products). Customers can select symptoms from the available options, which the rule-based decision tree evaluates to identify possible causes, determine the severity level, and suggest appropriate actions. The diagnostic results are saved in D6 (Fault Diagnostics). If the problem is classified as high-severity or cannot be resolved through the guided troubleshooting steps, the system creates a service ticket in D7 (Inquiry Logs) for staff follow-up.

**4.0 Admin and Staff Management**

This process provides a management panel with access based on user roles and permissions. The Admin can update product information, diagnostic rules, and system records, as well as access customer information and reports. Meanwhile, Staff can manage order approvals, respond to inquiries, and monitor urgent service requests. The process retrieves and updates relevant information in data stores D1 to D7 according to the user's authorized access. It also uses D8 (Profiles) to verify admin and staff accounts and determine their assigned permissions. In addition to printing the thermal QR receipt, the POS module dispatches an account confirmation email containing the rendered QR access pass and itemized warranty receipt.

		

| ID | Data Store | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| D1 | Products | Contains the product catalog, including product name, category, brand, wattage, battery specifications, waterproof rating, price, stock availability, recommended usage, suitable location, warranty details, and image URL. This information is accessed by the product matching and request processes and maintained through Process 4.0.  |
| D2 | Product Matching Logs | Stores the results of product matching sessions, including the customer's budget, usage type, location type, power requirements, and the IDs of recommended products.  |
| D3 | Order & Order Items | Contains customer  quote requests and order information, such as order status, total amount, scheduled pickup, approving staff member, and individual order items with their quantities, unit prices, and subtotals.  |
| D4 | Customers | Stores customer profile information, including name, email address, phone number, home address, dashboard UUID, and records of agreement to the terms of service and Data Privacy Act requirements.  |
| D5 | Customer Products | Records the products owned by each customer, including product details, serial number, installation date, warranty start and end dates, ownership status, and product condition.  |
| D6 | Fault Diagnostics | Keeps records of troubleshooting activities, including selected symptoms, possible causes, severity levels, recommended actions, escalation status, and additional customer notes.  |
| D7 | Inquiry Logs | Stores customer inquiries and service tickets, including inquiry type, subject, message, current status, assigned staff member, and admin response.  |
| D8 | Profiles (Admin Staff) | Contains admin and staff account details, such as name, email, phone number, assigned role, and account status. These records support authentication and role-based access control.  |
| D9 | Email Confirmation Queue | Holds queued, pending, and completed email transmission for auditing customer receipt dispatches. |

## **4.4 Software Testing Plan** {#4.4-software-testing-plan}

The system is tested at three distinct levels, Unit Testing checks individual functions, decision tree logic, and UI components in isolation; Integration Testing verifies data flow and communication protocols between the React frontend, REST APIs, and Supabase PostgreSQL database policies; and System Testing evaluates the end-to-end web platform across desktop and mobile devices from start to finish. Each testing level is conducted in a controlled environment that never touches the live production catalog or real customer records, operating strictly under zero online payment exposure. 

| Level | What is Tested | Tools | Environment | Who |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Unit | Individual JavaScript logic modules (multiCriteriaMatcher.js SAW scoring, solarDiagnosticEngine.js 4-pillar decision tree, sanitize.js XSS filters) and isolated React components. | Vitest, React Testing Library, ESLint | Local developer workstation (Vite dev server with isolated mock data) | Developers / Research Team  |
| Integration | Data pipelines between React frontend and Supabase API, Row Level Security (RLS) database policies, JWT role authentication, QUOTE\_TICKETS generation, and warranty pre-population handoffs. | Postman API Client, Supabase CLI, Browser DevTools | Dedicated Supabase test project environment | Developers / System Integrator |
| System | Complete end-to-end user journeys (product matching survey $\rightarrow$ O2O quote ticket $\rightarrow$ UUID dashboard access $\rightarrow$ guided fault diagnosis $\rightarrow$ staff escalation), cross-device responsiveness, and route security.  | Written test cases executed manually across desktop and mobile viewports (Chrome, Safari, Edge, Firefox)  | Deployed staging build on Vercel connected to test database (zero payment processing)  | Development team, Capstone Adviser, Business Owner, Showroom Staff, and Survey Respondents  |

#### **Table 12 \- Software Testing Plan** {#table-12---software-testing-plan}

### **4.4.1 Unit Testing** {#4.4.1-unit-testing}

 Focuses on evaluating individual software components, algorithms, decision tree logic, and user interface modules in isolation\[1\]. The objective of this testing phase is to verify that each isolated function produces exact expected outputs for given inputs, adheres to business logic constraints, and executes without runtime exceptions\]. In accordance with the project's technical specifications, unit testing was conducted on local developer workstations using Vitest alongside React Testing Library for component logic, while static code analysis and syntax enforcement were performed using ESLint

| Test Case ID | Target Module / Function | Test Input / Condition | Expected Output / Behavior | Actual Result | Status |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| UT-01  | multiCriteriaMatcher.js (SAW Composite Scoring) | Budget Score \= 0.98, Location Score \= 1.00, Power Score \= 1.00; Weights \= 0.35, 0.35, 0.30  | Calculated score equals 0.993 (99.3% match)  | Composite score calculated accurately at 99.3%  |  |
| UT-02  | multiCriteriaMatcher.js (Stock Penalty Filter) | Product composite match score \= 0.994; warehouse stock\_quantity \= 0  | Final score reduced by 50% to 0.497 (49.7%)  | Score penalized to 49.7% and demoted below recommendation threshold  |  |
| UT-03  | multiCriteriaMatcher.js (Threshold Gate) | Candidate product calculated match score \= 0.65 (65%)  | Product rejected and excluded from user recommendation list (\< 70%)  | Product excluded from final results  |  |
| UT-04  | solarDiagnosticEngine.js (4-Pillar Scorecard) | Electrical \= FAIL, Physical \= PASS, Env \= PASS, Control \= PASS  | Returns composite diagnostic scorecard with 30% Electrical failure weight  | Scorecard generated with exact pillar weight attribution  |  |
| UT-05  | solarDiagnosticEngine.js (Priority Elimination) | Selected symptom \+ optical lens moisture/condensation detected  | Immediate trigger of FLT-IP-009 (Water Ingress) override  | Priority rule bypassed standard runtime triage and outputted safety verdict  |  |
| UT-06  | solarDiagnosticEngine.js (Keyword Token Match) | Natural language text: "ayaw bumukas sa gabi"  | Auto-routes query to SYMPTOM\_NO\_POWER diagnostic branch  | Keyword tokens matched and correctly routed  |  |
| UT-07  | sanitize.js (XSS Stripping) | Input: \<script\>alert("XSS")\</script\>Solar Light | Output: "Solar Light" (tags and script content stripped)  | All HTML/XML tags and script content removed  |  |
| UT-08  | sanitize.js (Phone Normalization) | Input: " 0917-123-4567 " | Output: "09171234567" (isValid \= true) | Whitespace and dashes stripped; normalized to 11 digits |  |
| UT-09  | sanitize.js (Serial Number Clamp) | Input: "SN-2026\_001; DROP TABLE products;" | Output: "SN-2026\_001" | Non-alphanumeric/hyphen/underscore characters stripped  |  |
| UT-10 | buildAccountCreationEmailHtml & buildInquiryTicketEmailHtml | Input: Customer object with purchases array and base64 QR data URL. | Output: Generates compliant, industrial HTML containing monospace ticket/token, itemized equipment table. | Formatted HTML produced matching all design standards. |  |

### **4.4.2 Integration Testing** {#4.4.2-integration-testing}

Integration Testing evaluates the data transfer, communication protocols, and interface integrity between interconnected software modules, cloud REST API endpoints, and the Supabase PostgreSQL database engine. While Unit Testing verifies isolated client-side logic, Integration Testing confirms that the React frontend application correctly exchanges data with backend cloud services, enforces database security policies, and executes multi-module state transitions\]. Testing was conducted using the Postman API Client, Supabase CLI, and Browser DevTools connected to a dedicated Supabase staging environment operating under zero online payment exposure

| Test Case ID  | Parts Involved  | Scenario  | Expected Result  |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| IT-01  | Product Catalog, Product Details  | Select a product from the catalog.  | The product details page displays the selected product's specifications, image, price range, and availability.  |
| IT-02  | Match Wizard, Recommendation Engine, Product Catalog  | Enter installation, lighting, and budget criteria.  | The system displays product recommendations matching the submitted criteria.  |
| IT-03  | Quote Request Form, Supabase Database, Staff Inquiries  | Submit a quote request with valid customer and product information.  | The request is saved and appears in the staff inquiries interface.  |
| IT-04  | Login, Authentication, Role-Based Access Control, Admin/Staff Dashboards  | Sign in as an administrator, staff member, or unauthorized user.  | Authorized users can access their permitted dashboard; unauthorized access is blocked or redirected.  |
| IT-05  | Staff Inventory Portal, Product Database, Product Catalog  | Update a product's stock quantity or availability.  | The updated inventory is saved and the product catalog reflects the current availability.  |
| IT-06  | Diagnostic Interface, Diagnostic Engine  | Complete a diagnostic flow by selecting symptoms and conditions.  | The system displays a diagnosis with relevant fault information and recommended next steps.  |
| IT-07 | RegisterSaleScreen, customerService.js, /api/send-confirmation-email, Gmail SMTP. | Staff submits POS in-store sale with customer mobile number and valid email address. | Customer record and purchases are written to Supabase (customer\_purchases); API triggers SMTP transport and returns status awaiting\_confirmation with message ID. |
| IT-08 | QuoteModal.jsx, quote\_tickets table, /api/send-confirmation-email. | Public visitor submits a store reservation or inquiry in QuoteModal with an email address. | Ticket is saved to PostgreSQL and an email pass with the ticket reference code is dispatched immediately to the customer's inbox. |
| IT-09 | Customer Portal (/portal), confirmCustomerEmailByToken, Supabase RPC. | Customer clicks Confirm Email link (?token=...\&confirm\_email=...) received in their inbox. | email\_confirmed flips from false to true, email\_confirmation\_status updates to 'confirmed', and portal unlocks full verified account features. |

#### **Table 13 \- Unit Testing** {#table-13---unit-testing-1}

### **4.4.3 System Testing** {#4.4.3-system-testing}

System Testing evaluates the complete, fully integrated web application as a unified system to verify compliance with functional, non-functional, security, and usability specifications. Unlike Unit Testing (isolated code functions) and Integration Testing (data communication between endpoints), System Testing executes end-to-end user workflows across real-world environments. Testing was conducted on a staging build deployed on Vercel connected to the Supabase cloud staging database, evaluating system performance across desktop, laptop, tablet, and mobile viewports across major web browsers (Google Chrome, Apple Safari, Microsoft Edge, and Mozilla Firefox)  
. 

| ID | Task  | Steps  | Expected Result  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

## **4.5 User Acceptance Testing (UAT) & Evaluation**

User Acceptance Testing (UAT) was conducted to evaluate the developed JD Solar system based on the experience and feedback of its intended users and technical evaluators. The evaluation focused on determining whether the system's features met the intended requirements and whether the platform was acceptable in terms of software quality.

The respondents were asked to access and evaluate the system using the features relevant to their assigned user category. These included the product catalog, multi-criteria product matching, rule-based inquiry assistance, Online-to-Offline (O2O) request process, fault diagnostic dashboard, and staff and administrator management panels.

After evaluating the system, respondents completed a structured questionnaire through Google Forms. Their responses were collected and used to assess the system's software quality and identify areas for improvement.

# **CHAPTER 5: Results and Discussion**

## **5.1 System Implementation**

The JD Solar Digital Product Guide and Management System is implemented as a cloud-integrated, cross-platform web application developed using React, Vite, and Tailwind CSS on the client tier, with Supabase (PostgreSQL, Supabase Authentication, Supabase Storage) serving as the backend-as-a-service infrastructure.

  ### **5.1.2 Core Modules Features and Functional Workflows**

  **![][image26]![][image27]![][image28]![][image29]**

  ##### **Figures 26 \- Solar Product Matcher** {#figures-26---solar-product-matcher}

  **Multi-Criteria Product Matching**

  The product matching subsystem implements the Simple Additive Weighting (SAW) algorithm to eliminate customer hesitation and assist clients.

* Input Normalization: The algorithm captures user criteria across three normalized parameters:  
* Criteria Weighting: Assigns predetermined weights reflecting industrial performance significance:  
* Threshold Gating and Stock Penalty: Products failing minimum criteria compatibility or falling below a 70% threshold are excluded. Units currently out of warehouse stock incur a 50% score penalty, preventing out-of-stock items from ranking above available inventory.  
* Safety Gating: The engine applies deterministic exclusion rules, ensuring standard grid-powered AC luminaires are never recommended as standalone off-grid solar equipment.

		![][image30]![][image31]![][image32]

##### **Figures 27 \- Inquiry Modal** {#figures-27---inquiry-modal}

**Online-to-Offline (O2O) Inquire Now**  
Recognizing that commercial solar lighting units represent high-involvement consultative purchases requiring physical inspection

* Customers select products from the catalog and click "Inquire”, opening.  
* The customer provides contact details, target installation address, project notes, and indicates whether they intend to visit the Quiapo or Cavite showroom.  
* Submitting the form records a new quotation ticket in the quote\_tickets table.  
* The system immediately dispatches an official Reservation Receipt Pass to the customer's email containing an itemized summary, store location maps, and scheduled consultation guidelines.

  **Fault Diagnostic and Troubleshooting** 

  When a customer experiences luminaire degradation or failure, the portal launches the interactive troubleshooting modal

  	![][image33]

  ##### **Figure 28 \- Step 1 \- Symptoms** {#figure-28---step-1---symptoms}

* Step 1 (Symptom Intake): The client selects observed symptoms from standardized categories: "No Power / Won't Turn On", "Battery / Rapid Discharge", "Dim Lighting / Low Output", "Sensor & Remote Control Malfunction", or "Physical Damage / Lens Condensation".

  ![][image34]

  ##### **Figure 29 \- Step 2 \- Electrical Check** {#figure-29---step-2---electrical-check}

* Step 2 (Electrical Check): Investigates charge controller LED status, charging voltage continuity, and photovoltaic panel wiring integrity.

  ![][image35]

  ##### **Figure 30 \- Step 3 \- Enclosure Check** {#figure-30---step-3---enclosure-check}

* Step 3 (Enclosure Check): Evaluates lens condensation, chassis water accumulation, and silicone gasket condition to detect IP65/IP67 ingress failures.

  ![][image36]

  ##### **Figure 31 \- Step 4 \- Environmental and Solar Exposure Assessment** {#figure-31---step-4---environmental-and-solar-exposure-assessment}

* Step 4 (Environmental and Solar Exposure Assessment): Assesses physical shading from tree canopies or structures, direct sunlight exposure hours (minimum 6--8 hours required), and surface dust/debris build-up on photovoltaic glass.

  ![][image37]

  ##### **Figure 32 \- Step 5 \- Diagnostic Verdict** {#figure-32---step-5---diagnostic-verdict}

* Step 5 (Diagnostic Verdict): Evaluates the inputs against deterministic decision paths, returning:  
  1. System Fault Code  
  2. Evaluated Scorecard (attributed weights: Electrical 30%, Seal 25%, Environmental 25%, Control 20%)  
  3. Severity Rating: High (Immediate Danger / Hardware Breakdown), Medium (Degraded Performance), or Low (Maintenance Required)  
  4. Critical Safety Warnings: Alerts clients to severe hazards (e.g., swollen lithium battery risk, short-circuit fire precautions) prior to suggesting physical handling.  
  5. Actionable Corrective Protocol: Distinguishes between user-executable maintenance (cleaning glass, clearing shading) and required bench repair.  
* Escalation to Service Ticket: If the fault is unresolvable or classified as severe, the user clicks "Submit Warranty Claim". The modal transitions into an integrated escalation form, automatically binding the scorecard and fault code to the customer's purchase ID, allowing photo/video upload, and submitting the record directly to the showroom triage pipeline.

			![][image38]

##### **Figure 33 \- Register Sale and QR Generator** {#figure-33---register-sale-and-qr-generator}

**In-Store POS Sale Registration and QR Pass Generator**  
To bridge walk-in showroom transactions with the digital customer portal:

* Attendants utilize Register sale to record point-of-sale cash or bank-transfer purchases.  
* Entering customer contact details generates or updates the customer record in the customers database table.  
* The system provisions a non-sequential, cryptographically random access token for the customer.  
* Upon saving, It generates a dynamic QR code encoding the unique customer portal URL. The QR code and transaction summary can be printed on physical thermal receipt slips or downloaded as digital PNG passes.

			![][image19]

##### **Figure 34 \- Kanban Warranty Claim and Triage** {#figure-34---kanban-warranty-claim-and-triage}

**Kanban Warranty Claim Triage**  
In the staff and administrator portals warranty claims submitted diagnostic claims are managed through a Kanban board:

* Diagnostic Intake: New claims submitted from the diagnostic modal appear immediately for bench triage. Staff review uploaded photographic evidence.  
* Approved for Release: Claims approved for hardware replacement or warranty repair transition to this stage, notifying showroom inventory to prepare replacement fixtures.  
* Handover Complete: Once the customer receives their repaired or replaced unit, the ticket is closed with an immutable resolution timestamp.  
* Declined: Claims violating warranty terms (e.g., physical tampering, intentional casing penetration, or post-expiration submissions) are declined with mandatory staff justification notes.  
  


  ## **5.2 Evaluation Results (ISO/IEC 25010\)**

A total of 47 respondents evaluated the system, comprising 22 IT students, 20 non-IT respondents (staff and retail customers), and 5 IT professionals. Non-IT evaluators assessed the operational characteristics directly relevant to end-user functions, while technical evaluators assessed all operational and architectural criteria.

  ### **5.2.1 Functional suitability**

| The troubleshooting diagnostic tool provides appropriate solutions based on the hardware problems selected. (Functional Correctness) | 4.53 | Strongly Agree |

  ## **5.3 Discussion of findings**


  This section interprets the evaluation data obtained from the 47 respondents across the nine software quality characteristics. The discussion examines how well the system fulfills its technical and business objectives, identifies operational strengths, and highlights specific areas for improvement.


  ### **5.3.1 Overall system evaluation**


  The evaluation of the JD Solar platform produced a Grand Weighted Mean of 4.62, corresponding to a verbal interpretation of Strongly Agree. This positive assessment demonstrates that respondents accept the platform as an effective solution for off-grid solar equipment selection, quotation inquiry, and post-purchase fault diagnostics.


  A closer examination across evaluator groups reveals consistent support from both technical and operational stakeholders:


  IT professionals awarded the highest overall mean rating of 4.80. This group validated the cloud database integration, modular code separation, and deterministic recommendation logic.


  IT students recorded a mean rating of 4.67. Their evaluation confirmed interface consistency, responsive layouts across devices, and clear navigation paths.


  Non-IT respondents (staff and retail customers) recorded a mean rating of 4.40. While lower than the technical groups, this rating remains firmly within the Strongly Agree category. It confirms that the system simplifies consultative inquiries and technical comparisons without overwhelming non-technical users.


  These findings validate the choice of an Agile development lifecycle. Iterative prototyping and user testing allowed the development team to refine UI layouts, streamline quote submission forms, and eliminate dead ends in the diagnostic decision trees before final evaluation.


  ### **5.3.2 Functional and operational quality**


  The core operational characteristics of the platform comprise Functional Suitability (4.57), Performance Efficiency (4.46), and Reliability (4.50).


  Under Functional Suitability (4.57), respondents gave the highest ratings (4.62) to the technical search and filter tools and the administrative dashboard. Evaluators verified that the Simple Additive Weighting (SAW) algorithm produces accurate recommendations based on installation location, mounting height, and wattage. The "Inquire Now" and "Inquire this" workflow received a rating of 4.53, confirming that customer quote requests capture essential site notes and contact information without data loss.


  Performance Efficiency scored 4.46. Catalog browsing and client-side page rendering operated with acceptable speed (4.53), and device resource utilization remained stable (4.53). Two items scored 4.38: the speed of recommendation generation and the time required to update stock availability in the database. When users submit complex diagnostic inputs or multiple search filters simultaneously, database query latency increases slightly. Pacing the conversational diagnostic engine with simulated text streaming helps user perception, but background network latency during write operations requires further caching.


  Reliability scored 4.50. System availability during testing scored 4.60, and database state preservation after page reloads scored 4.57. Fault tolerance scored 4.38. When evaluators entered invalid non-numeric inputs or disconnected their internet connection during form submission, the application displayed error alerts rather than crashing. However, several respondents noted that error messages on network timeouts should provide clearer instructions on whether to resubmit the inquiry or wait for connectivity to resume.

  ### **5.3.3 Compatibility and adaptability**

* Compatibility (4.78) and Flexibility (4.79) achieved the two highest criteria weighted means in the entire evaluation.  
* Compatibility scored 4.78. Technical evaluators verified that the Tailwind CSS responsive grid correctly adapts interface elements across smartphones, tablets, laptops, and desktop displays (4.81). Network switching between Wi-Fi and cellular mobile data scored 4.85, confirming that the Supabase client handles transport transitions smoothly. The platform also maintained stable rendering across Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge without broken buttons or misaligned specification cards (4.73).  
* Flexibility scored 4.79. Evaluators gave the highest individual score in this category (4.88) to the modifiability of the recommendation logic. Because the matching parameters reside in externalized rule arrays rather than hard-coded conditional blocks, developers can introduce new product lines (such as hybrid inverters or solar batteries) without altering core display logic. Parameter configurability (such as updating local electricity tariff rates used in cost-recovery calculations) scored 4.85. Cloud database scalability scored 4.81, indicating confidence that PostgreSQL handles growing transaction logs as the business expands.


  ### **5.3.4 Security, safety, and maintainability**

    
* Security, safety, and maintainability represent the operational safeguards and architectural health of the platform.  
* Security scored 4.60. Evaluators rated public page restrictions highest at 4.70. Row Level Security (RLS) policies in Supabase prevent unauthorized visitors from viewing staff dashboard routes or accessing protected customer records. Administrative deletion permissions scored 4.62, and customer data privacy scored 4.62. Unauthorized price modification protection scored 4.49. Evaluators verified that role checks run on the server side, preventing client-side script inspection from modifying catalog prices.  
* Maintainability scored 4.74. IT professionals and students commended the component modularity (4.69) and testability of independent functions (4.77). Separating the business logic into distinct service modules (solarBotEngine.js, solarDiagnosticEngine.js) allows developers to update recommendation formulas without affecting inventory tables. Error logging and console tracing scored 4.77, simplifying bug isolation during development.  
* Safety scored 4.49. The system enforces input validation to prevent incomplete catalog entries (4.51). Safety warnings displayed in the fault diagnostic tool scored 4.47, and website installation reminders scored 4.53. In off-grid solar equipment, physical risks such as swollen lithium iron phosphate cells or short circuits require caution. The diagnostic modal issues explicit warnings before directing users to perform physical hardware checks, preventing accidental exposure to electrical hazards.


  ### **5.3.5 User interaction and areas for improvement**

    
  Interaction Capability achieved a favorable rating of 4.64. Evaluators praised the clarity of product specification cards (4.70), clean typographical labels (4.68), and visible UI feedback states (4.68). The two-column specification layout allows buyers to review critical technical metrics (wattage, battery capacity, lumen output, IP water-resistance rating) quickly.  
    
  Despite these positive ratings, several areas require improvement based on individual scores:  
    
* Fault tolerance under disconnected states (4.38). When internet connectivity drops while submitting an inquiry, the form alerts the user but does not retain entered text in local storage if the user navigates away. Adding local browser caching will protect customer entries during intermittent connections.  
* Inventory update response speed (4.38). Updating inventory counts in the admin portal currently requires a synchronous round trip to the database. Introducing optimistic UI updates will give staff immediate visual confirmation while the database syncs in the background.  
* Diagnostic recommendation speed (4.38). The simulated AI streaming engine introduces intentional typing pauses to deliver an organic conversational feel. For experienced users seeking quick answers, adding a "Skip Pacing" button will let them view the complete diagnostic verdict immediately.  
* User guidance and onboarding (4.57). First-time visitors unfamiliar with technical solar terms (e.g., monocrystalline versus polycrystalline, depth of discharge, color rendering index) would benefit from contextual tooltip definitions when hovering over technical badges.

# **Chapter 6: Summary, conclusions, and recommendations**

## **6.1 Summary of findings**

This study addressed the operational bottlenecks faced by JD Solar, a retail business specializing in off-grid solar lighting systems. The business previously conducted customer consultations, product recommendations, and after-sales troubleshooting through manual social media messaging. This manual approach caused response delays, customer confusion regarding technical specifications, and administrative fatigue.

To resolve these problems, the researchers designed and developed JD Solar, a web-based e-commerce platform incorporating rule-based multi-criteria product matching and fault diagnostic workflows. The application features:

* A multi-criteria matching wizard (JD Solar Assistant) that uses the Simple Additive Weighting (SAW) algorithm to match customer budget, installation location, and illumination requirements with suitable solar luminaires.  
* An interactive rule-based survey structured around the five customer consultation pillars: Product Specifications, Pricing and Budgeting, Stock Availability, Installation Requirements, and Warranty and Support.  
* An Online-to-Offline (O2O) quote reservation system ("Inquire this" / "Inquire Now") that records customer requests and issues consultation passes for physical showroom inspection.  
* A rule-based fault diagnostic engine that evaluates hardware symptoms across four technical pillars (Electrical, Enclosure Seals, Environmental Shading, and Sensor Controls) to generate fault scorecards and safety warnings.  
* Administrative and staff management portals for inventory stock tracking, inquiry review, and warranty claim management.  
    
  A formal evaluation was conducted with 47 respondents, consisting of 22 IT students, 20 non-IT respondents (staff and consumers), and 5 IT professionals, using the nine quality characteristics of the ISO/IEC 25010:2023 software quality model. The evaluation yielded a Grand Weighted Mean of 4.62, interpreted as Strongly Agree.  
    
  The individual criteria weighted means were:  
    
* Flexibility: 4.79 (Strongly Agree)  
* Compatibility: 4.78 (Strongly Agree)  
* Maintainability: 4.74 (Strongly Agree)  
* Interaction Capability: 4.64 (Strongly Agree)  
* Security: 4.60 (Strongly Agree)  
* Functional Suitability: 4.57 (Strongly Agree)  
* Reliability: 4.50 (Strongly Agree)  
* Safety: 4.49 (Strongly Agree)  
* Performance Efficiency: 4.46 (Strongly Agree)


  All nine quality characteristics achieved verbal interpretations of Strongly Agree, indicating high acceptance across both technical and non-technical stakeholders.


  ## **6.2 Conclusions**


  Based on the development, implementation, and empirical evaluation of the JD Solar platform, the researchers reached the following conclusions:

    
* The multi-criteria product matching engine successfully converts customer requirements into accurate solar luminaire recommendations. Incorporating the Simple Additive Weighting method and deterministic exclusion rules prevents mismatched recommendations (such as suggesting grid-powered AC lights for off-grid outdoor applications).  
* The Online-to-Offline (O2O) inquiry workflow bridges digital browsing with physical showroom transactions. By replacing traditional e-commerce shopping carts with consultative "Inquire Now" requests, the platform respects the industrial nature of solar equipment and avoids customer purchasing errors.  
* The rule-based fault diagnostic module automates initial troubleshooting for common solar luminaire failures. The four-pillar scorecard provides customers with clear, structured explanations of battery degradation, water ingress, and panel shading while issuing necessary safety warnings before suggesting physical hardware inspection.  
* The cloud database architecture and role-based access control policies maintain data integrity and operational confidentiality. Restricting administrative actions to authenticated personnel ensures that inventory levels, customer contact details, and price records remain protected against unauthorized modification.  
* The developed platform satisfies the software quality requirements defined by the ISO/IEC 25010:2023 standard, as evidenced by the Grand Weighted Mean of 4.62. The system achieves its primary objective of providing JD Solar with an automated, reliable, and accessible platform for off-grid solar equipment selection and after-sales support.


  ## **6.3 Recommendations**


  Based on the evaluation findings and technical limitations identified during the study, the researchers offer the following recommendations:


  **For JD Solar management and staff**

* Establish a dedicated showroom tablet or terminal running the staff dashboard to monitor incoming quote inquiries and warranty tickets during business hours.  
* Conduct regular staff training on reviewing diagnostic scorecards and customer photo attachments submitted through the troubleshooting portal to accelerate bench triage.  
* Maintain stable showroom internet connectivity to prevent delays during real-time database updates and inventory synchronization.  
* Regularly update product pricing, stock quantities, and electricity tariff parameters in the administrative panel to maintain recommendation accuracy.  
  **For future developers and researchers**  
* Implement local browser caching (such as IndexedDB or localStorage) to store customer form inputs during temporary network interruptions, preventing data loss when internet connectivity drops.  
* Integrate optimistic UI updates within the inventory management dashboard so that staff receive immediate interface confirmation while write requests complete in the background.  
* Introduce an option to toggle or bypass simulated text streaming in the diagnostic engine for returning users who prefer instant results over conversational pacing.  
* Add contextual explanatory tooltips and glossary popovers for technical solar specifications (such as IP ingress ratings, battery chemistry, and lumen decay) to assist first-time buyers.  
* Integrate an SMS or automated email notification service to alert customers when their quotation ticket has been reviewed or when their warranty claim status changes.  
* Explore progressive web application (PWA) caching and offline service workers to allow field installers and remote customers to access diagnostic manuals even without internet access.  
* Integrate IoT telemetry or bluetooth charge controller logging to allow solar streetlights to upload battery voltage and charging metrics directly into the diagnostic engine.
